title: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: ClickOnce
shortTitle: Trusted Developer Utilities Proxy Execution: ClickOnce
summary: ClickOnce is a Microsoft deployment technology for self-updating Windows applications built on the .NET platform, which install and run from a web page or a file share with minimal user interaction. This sub-technique covers its abuse as an execution proxy. An .appref-ms or .application file points at a deployment manifest, and the signed DFSVC.EXE component installs and launches the application as its child process. Because ClickOnce applications request only limited permissions, no administrator rights are needed, so the technique works on ordinary user accounts. A common chain leans on user execution: the victim opens a link or a startup folder entry and a familiar installation prompt appears. Defenders see dfsvc.exe, or rundll32 loading the dfshim component, fetching a deployment from an unfamiliar host, and a deployment file placed in a startup folder where it will run again at each sign in.

beginner.definition: ClickOnce is a Microsoft way to install and update programs. Those programs are built with the .NET platform, a Microsoft development framework. The program can start from a web page or a shared folder. The parent technique covers trusted developer tools in general. This sub-technique is the ClickOnce case, where a small deployment file starts the program.
beginner.whyItMatters: ClickOnce programs install without administrator rights, so any user account can run one. The installer is a signed Microsoft component, so it is usually trusted by security tools. A user only has to click a normal looking prompt, which makes the attack easy to deliver. Because the program can update itself later, the attacker can change what it does.
howItWorks: The attacker hosts a deployment file, such as an .application or .appref-ms file, on a website or a share.
The user opens that file, for example by clicking a link or a file that arrived in a message.
The ClickOnce component DFSVC.EXE reads the file and fetches the application from the given location.
The program starts as a child process of DFSVC.EXE and runs with only limited permissions.
No administrator rights are needed, so the installation usually succeeds on a normal user account.
The program can also update itself later on. Copying the deployment file into a startup folder makes it run again after each sign in.
beginner.example: Imagine a vending machine in an office corridor that restocks itself from the supplier. Anyone can walk up and press a button, with no key and no permission from the office manager. The machine looks official and the corridor is public. If somebody changes what the supplier sends, the same button now delivers something completely different.
takeaways: ClickOnce installs without administrator rights, so standard accounts are a target.
The launched program appears as a child of DFSVC.EXE, which is a useful detection point.
A deployment file placed in a startup folder means the program runs again after every sign in.

objectives: Explain what ClickOnce is and how a deployment file starts an application.
Describe how this sub-technique differs from its parent technique.
Explain why ClickOnce does not require administrator rights.
Identify the processes and network connections involved in a ClickOnce launch.
Describe how a deployment file in a startup folder gives repeated execution.
